title: The Ingredients of an Effective Performance Improvement Plan (PIP)
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay outlines what separates a genuine performance improvement plan from one used as a pretext for termination. It argues good-faith PIPs share specific ingredients: clearly stated goals and timelines, explicitly stated consequences rather than implied threats, very specific and sequenced action steps small enough to be achievable, named resources or mentors to support the effort, and defined check-in dates over the typical 30-, 60-, or 90-day window. The piece is candid that even well-constructed PIPs sometimes reveal that a team member's deficiencies can't be overcome, but insists the structure itself must be built as a genuine attempt at improvement, not a documented off-ramp.
points: Distinguishes good-faith PIPs (genuine improvement roadmaps) from PIPs used as documentation on the way to a predetermined termination.
Specifies that consequences must be explicitly stated in a PIP, not left implied or presumed.
Argues the most important PIP ingredient is a sequence of small, specific, individually achievable action steps.
Recommends naming concrete support resources — mentors, colleagues, experts — inside the plan itself.
Notes typical PIP timelines run 30, 60, or 90 days and require explicit scheduled check-in dates to be taken seriously.
quotes: Leaders often require team members who are underperforming in a critical area to agree to such a personalized map for self-improvement. For those in Human Resources, such a structured plan is typically called a PIP (Performance Improvement Plan).

In the best cases, they are a detailed and achievable roadmap for improvement. In the worst cases, PIPs represent a last-ditch effort to prove to the individual that they are not up to the tasks the team requires of them.
Perhaps the most important part of the plan is the action steps outlined for improvement. The best PIPs have very specific tasks, experiences, or actionable steps that are often ordered in sequence.
Any resources to support and aid in the team member’s improvement should be spelled out. In many cases, other team members, mentors, or experts are made available to assist their colleague.
Lastly, an effective PIP should specify when the leader will check in to track progress. Dates and times for these checkpoints are essential for everyone to take the process seriously.
